key: Provisional Measure 1.394 of 25 September 2026 prohibits fixed-odds betting across Brazil: sports betting and online casino games alike.
The licensed .bet.br sites had to go offline from 6 October. Remaining balances go back to players through their banks between 9 and 14 October.
The ban reaches operators based abroad that offer bets to people in Brazil, which includes crypto casinos.
The measure lapses unless Congress converts it into law within 60 days, a period that can be extended once by another 60.
body: Brazil's government published Provisional Measure 1.394 on 25 September 2026. It prohibits, across the whole country, the operation, offer, intermediation and advertising of fixed-odds betting. Fixed-odds betting is the legal category that covered both sports betting and online casino games in Brazil's licensed market.
## What the ban covers

According to the Ministry of Finance, the measure applies to sports bets and to online games, in physical and virtual settings alike. It applies even when an operator based abroad offers them to people located in Brazil. It also covers the concessions, permits and authorisations that states and the Federal District had granted for fixed-odds betting. Other lotteries authorised by law are not affected.
## The timetable
From 25 September, no new money could go into betting accounts. Players had until 23:59 on 5 October to request their balances. From 6 October, betting sites and apps had to be unavailable.

On 6 and 7 October, operators must report each player's remaining balance to the banks, listed by CPF and with the bank account the deposits came from. The banks return the money between 9 and 14 October. Where a bank cannot, Caixa Econômica Federal acts as intermediary from 14 October.
## What happened to the licensed market

Brazil opened its licensed market on 1 January 2025, with every authorised operator on a .bet.br domain. The Secretariat of Prizes and Bets (SPA) still publishes its list of the companies it authorised, now titled as authorised until the measure took effect, but none of them may operate. Our licensed-casinos page lists Brazil as a market with no legal operators for that reason.
## What it means for crypto casinos

Licensed operators were already barred from taking crypto deposits under SPA Ordinance 615 of 2024. The new measure goes further: offering bets or online casino games to people in Brazil is prohibited, whoever the operator is and wherever it is based. A crypto casino that leaves Brazil off its own restricted list is not thereby lawful to play at from Brazil. Our Brazil country pages now lead with the ban.
## How long it lasts

A provisional measure has the force of law from the day it is published. Under Article 62 of the Constitution, it lapses unless Congress converts it into law within 60 days, a period that can be extended once by another 60. We will update the Brazil pages when Congress acts.

key: Studios can license one title at several return rates
The casino chooses which build it runs
The in-game paytable is the only reliable source
body: A slot is not one machine. Most volume studios ship a title in two or three configurations — typically a headline rate and one or two reduced builds — and the operator picks which it licenses. Nothing in the lobby tells you which one you loaded.

The paytable inside the game does. It states the return for the build you are playing, and it is the figure RTP Watch records, per casino, as our field-testing reaches each operator. Where a reading shows a reduced build we name it in that operator's review rather than the studio's.
Two points of return is not a rounding difference. On $10,000 of turnover it is $200 of expected value moved from you to the house, for exactly the same game and the same session length.

key: Multiply the credit, not the deposit
Game weighting can double the real figure
A max-cashout cap can make the whole offer worthless
body: Wagering is stated as a multiple of the credited amount. At 40× a $100 bonus needs $4,000 of turnover before withdrawal; at 1× it needs $100. That single number moves an offer from useful to unusable, and it is the first thing to find in the terms.

Then read the weighting. If slots count 100% but live tables count 10%, the same requirement takes ten times the volume at a blackjack table. Bonuses that exclude sportsbook entirely are common and rarely stated in the headline.

Finally check the cap. A max cashout of 5× the bonus means a $100 credit can never return more than $500 no matter what you hit, which quietly deletes the tail of the distribution you were playing for.

key: Tiered verification is the norm, not the exception
Cumulative volume is usually the trigger
Verify before you need to, not after a win
body: Most crypto casinos run tiered verification: you can deposit, play and withdraw small amounts unverified, and a document request appears once cumulative volume crosses a threshold. The threshold is rarely published, and an operator can move it without notice.
Withdrawal is the worst moment to discover it. A cash-out routed to verification is one of the most common reasons a payout takes a day instead of minutes.
If you intend to play at any size, verify on a quiet day. It takes a few minutes and removes a common source of withdrawal delay.

key: Seconds to credit, no on-chain fee
Channel capacity caps the amount
Few operators support it, so check the cashier
body: Lightning settles in seconds and avoids on-chain fees entirely, which makes it the correct rail for small, frequent deposits. Where an operator supports it, it is usually the quickest way to a playable balance in bitcoin.
The constraint is capacity. Larger payments are more likely to hit channel limits, and when they do the payment fails rather than arriving slowly, which is confusing the first time it happens.
Support is thin. Each casino profile lists the coins and networks the operator itself names, so check there, and in the cashier, before relying on Lightning.

key: Policies differ by casino, so read the profile
It matters most on small, frequent cash-outs
Chain choice moves it by two orders of magnitude
body: A withdrawal fee deducted from your balance is a real cost, and it compounds if you cash out often. Some operators say they cover the network fee; others pass it through, and some charge a fixed per-coin fee on top. Each casino profile quotes the operator's own wording on withdrawal fees.

The chain matters more than the policy. An Ethereum withdrawal can cost dollars in gas at busy times; the same transfer on Solana costs a fraction of a cent. A fee-absorbing operator on an expensive chain can still be the worse deal.
The coins page explains how each network sets its fee. Check the operator's own withdrawal fee in its cashier before you pick a chain.

key: Hot wallet for play, cold wallet for holdings
Never fund a casino from an exchange address
Assume any on-site balance can be frozen
body: Keep the amount you are willing to lose in a hot wallet, and everything else somewhere that requires a deliberate act to reach. Operators freeze accounts for routine verification more often than players expect, and a frozen balance is out of reach until it clears.
Do not send from an exchange to a cashier directly. Casino addresses are clustered by analytics firms, and the return path is what triggers compliance questions on your exchange account later.
Treat any balance on-site as in transit. The account is a place to play, not a place to keep money.

key: Six areas, every fact cited
Commission is not an input
Gaps are marked, not guessed
body: Every review covers the same six areas: payout speed, bonus fairness, crypto support, trust and licensing, game and RTP quality, and support. There is no score or weighting. A review states what the operator publishes on each, with a citation, so you can check it yourself.
Commercial relationships are not an input. We earn commission when a reader signs up through our links, and the rate is not visible to whoever writes the review. It never changes what a review says.
Where an operator doesn't publish something, the profile says "Not stated" instead of filling the gap with a guess.

key: Margin is the overround baked into the price
Compare across many markets, not one
One point of margin beats any welcome offer
body: Margin, or overround, is the amount by which a book's implied probabilities exceed 100%. It is the sportsbook equivalent of RTP, and unlike a bonus it applies to every bet you place.

To compare books fairly, take the same markets across football, basketball, tennis and esports, at the same time of day, and look at the median rather than one price. Books quote tighter on marquee events and wider on everything else, so a single-market comparison is misleading.
A book a point tighter costs you less over a season than any promotion returns. It is the least visible and most important number on a sportsbook.

key: KYC is the document check that stands between you and your money
Only one of {casinos} operators says it will never run one
The tier an operator sits in is set by its own terms, not its marketing
body: KYC — know your customer — is the point where a casino stops treating you as an anonymous balance and asks who you are. Usually a government ID, often a selfie, sometimes a utility bill. It exists because the licence requires it: an operator that cannot show it checked is an operator that can lose the licence.

For a crypto casino the interesting question is not whether KYC exists. It is when it fires. You can deposit, play and win without ever being asked, and then be asked at the moment you try to take the money out — which is the worst time to discover your name does not match your ID.

We read the stated policy at all {casinos} casinos we track and sorted them by what the policy actually does. {required} make verification a step you complete before you can play or withdraw. {threshold} publish a trigger — a cumulative deposit figure, a withdrawal size, a deadline after your first deposit — so you can see it coming. {discretionary} run no routine check but reserve the right to ask, usually at withdrawal or on anything that looks unusual. {conflicting} contradict themselves across their own pages. And {never} says it will never ask at all.

The tier is not the same as the marketing. Razed calls itself a No-KYC crypto casino; its own AML policy requests ID documents when you withdraw. Bluff usually asks for nothing — unless you opt into a bonus, which makes verification a condition. Degencity lets you deposit, play and withdraw without documents but still wants a verified email address before it pays. Read the second sentence of any no-KYC claim; that is where the conditions live.

What this means in practice: decide before you deposit, not after. If you will not hand over a passport, an operator in the required tier is not for you whatever its bonus looks like — you will hit the wall at cash-out. If you are fine with verification, do it early and on a quiet day rather than at the moment you are trying to withdraw a win. And if an operator's pages disagree with each other, assume the stricter one applies, because that is the one its compliance team works from.

key: Check whether you are eligible before you deposit, not after
Verify on a quiet day — the worst time to start is mid-withdrawal
{threshold} operators publish the exact figure that triggers a check
body: Verification is the step where a casino stops treating you as a balance and asks who you are. It is also where money gets stuck, almost always for the same reason: the account was opened in a hurry, the details did not match the documents, and nobody found out until a withdrawal was already in flight.

**Start with eligibility, before you deposit anything.** Two separate things have to be true. Your country has to allow you to play — that is the law where you are, and it is not the operator's decision. And the operator has to accept your country, which is in its own terms. They disagree more often than you would think: nine countries we cover ban online casinos while most operators' terms do not mention them at all. Our legal map has the first answer and each casino page has the second. Getting this wrong is the one mistake that cannot be fixed later, because a balance built in a place you were never allowed to play is a balance you will not be paid.

**Register with the details that are on your documents.** Legal name as spelled on the ID, date of birth, address as it appears on a recent bill or statement. Not a nickname, not an old address, not a middle name you usually drop. Every mismatch is a manual review, and manual reviews happen at the slowest possible moment. One account per person, in your own name — paying a balance to someone whose name is not on the account is the thing compliance teams are built to stop.

**Then verify, and do it early.** Of the {casinos} casinos we track, {required} make verification a step you complete before you can play or withdraw, and {threshold} publish the figure that triggers it — Cloudbet at $2,200 of cumulative deposits, FortuneJack at $10,000, Winna within 30 days of your first deposit or €2,000 wagered, mBit above 1 BTC. Another {discretionary} run no routine check and reserve the right to ask anyway, usually at the moment you withdraw. Only one says it never will. So the question is not whether you can avoid it; it is whether you do it on a quiet Tuesday or during a cash-out.

**What to have ready.** A government photo ID, usually both sides. A selfie, sometimes holding the document — seven operators ask for one and one wants it from five angles. Proof of address dated within the last three months, which thirteen ask for: a utility bill or bank statement, not a screenshot of an app. Where larger sums are involved you may be asked for source of funds, which means showing where the money came from rather than just who you are. Photograph documents flat, in daylight, with all four corners in frame and nothing cropped — most rejections are a corner out of shot, not a problem with the document.

**Submit through the account itself, never anywhere else.** Open verification from inside your own logged-in session. No legitimate operator asks for identity documents over live chat, email, Telegram, Discord or a link someone sends you, and anyone who does is not the casino. Some route the check through a third-party provider — Duel uses Checkin.com, Solcasino uses Sumsub — which is normal, but you should still arrive there from inside your account rather than from a link.

**If it stalls.** Most delays are a document that was readable to you and not to a reviewer: a glare, a cropped edge, an address that no longer matches. Resubmit a cleaner copy before assuming anything is wrong. If a check is taking longer than the operator's own stated time, ask support through the account and keep the thread. And read the bonus terms before you opt in rather than after — Bluff needs no verification to withdraw unless you took a bonus, at which point it does.

key: Check you are allowed to play before you create anything
Use the details that are on your ID — mismatches surface at cash-out
The bonus decision is made at your first deposit and is usually final
body: Signing up takes about two minutes and sets four things you will live with. Most people get three of them wrong by doing it quickly, and only find out weeks later when a withdrawal stalls.

**Is it legal where you are?** Not whether the casino will take you — those are different questions and they disagree often. Nine of the countries we cover ban online casinos while most operators' terms do not mention them at all, so a sign-up page that lets you through is not permission. Check the law first on our legal map, then check the operator's own restricted list on its page here. If either says no, stop: a balance built where you were never allowed to play is a balance that will not be paid out.

**Email or wallet?** Most of the {casinos} casinos we track open an account on an email address and a password. A few are wallet-first — Goated starts at an email or a connected wallet, MetaWin runs on one. Wallet sign-up is faster and gives the operator less about you up front, but it moves the burden: lose the wallet and you lose the account, and there is no password reset for a key you no longer have.

**Enter the details that are on your documents.** Legal name as spelled on the ID, real date of birth, the address on a recent bill. This is the step that quietly decides how your first withdrawal goes, because {required} of the {casinos} make verification a condition of playing or withdrawing and the rest reserve the right to ask. Every mismatch between the account and the document is a manual review, and reviews land at the worst moment. One account, in your own name — an operator will not pay a balance to a name that is not on the account.

**Decide about the bonus before you deposit, not after.** Opting in is usually irreversible for that deposit, and it changes the account's rules rather than just adding money: wagering has to clear before anything can leave, and at some operators it pulls in obligations that were not there before. Bluff needs no verification to withdraw at all — unless you took a bonus, at which point it does. Read the wagering multiplier and what counts toward it first; our bonuses page has every one we hold, each from the operator's own terms.

**Then verify, while nothing is at stake.** You do not have to wait to be asked. Doing it on a quiet day with good light and a clean copy of your ID costs ten minutes; doing it mid-withdrawal costs however long the queue is, at the one moment you care. The KYC guide covers what each operator asks for and which publish the figure that triggers a check.

key: The network matters more than the coin — the wrong one loses the funds
All {casinos} take BTC, ETH and USDT; the long tail is where support thins out
Send a small test first, every time, to a new address
body: A crypto deposit is one irreversible instruction. There is no chargeback, no support ticket that reverses it, and no bank to call. Almost everything that goes wrong goes wrong in the thirty seconds before you press send.

**The coin is the easy part.** All {casinos} casinos we track credit Bitcoin, Ethereum and USDT. After that it thins: 42 take Litecoin, 40 Solana, 38 Tron, 34 Dogecoin and 34 XRP. If you hold something further out, check the operator's own coin list before you move anything, because an unsupported coin sent to a deposit address is not a deposit — it is a loss.

**The network is the hard part, and it is where money actually disappears.** USDT is not one thing. The same stablecoin runs on Ethereum as ERC-20, on Tron as TRC-20, on BNB Smart Chain, on Polygon, on Solana. Sportsbet.io's own page lists four chains for USDT and five for USDC. Pick the network on the casino's deposit screen first, then pick the matching one in your wallet — never the other way round. Sending TRC-20 USDT to an ERC-20 address is the single most common way to lose a deposit, and it is unrecoverable.

**Copy the address, then check it.** Always copy and paste, never retype. Then read the first four and last four characters against the screen before sending, because clipboard-hijacking malware exists precisely for this moment. Deposit addresses can rotate between visits, so use the one shown now rather than one you saved.

**Send a small test to any address you have not used before.** The smallest amount the operator will credit, confirmed arrived, then the real amount. It costs one extra network fee and it is the only way to find out you had the network wrong while it still costs almost nothing. Minimums are low enough that this is cheap: Shuffle credits from $0.01, and {noMinimum} operators including Roobet, Stake and Duelbits state no crypto minimum at all. Rollbit sets its by coin — $5 for stablecoins, 0.0001 BTC, 0.002 ETH.

**Then wait for confirmations.** The casino credits after a set number of blocks, not instantly, and that number is theirs to choose. Minutes on a fast chain, longer on Bitcoin when it is busy. A deposit that has not appeared is almost always still confirming — check the transaction on a block explorer with the hash your wallet gave you before contacting anyone. Who pays the network fee, and how to cut it, is its own guide.

key: 8 of the 46 crypto casinos we track name Brazil on their restricted lists, two weeks after Brazil banned online betting and casino games.
25 publish a full restricted list that leaves Brazil off. We re-read 12 of those on 8 October 2026; Brazil was on none of them.
One casino, Gamba, says on its own page that its services are available to users in Brazil.
A casino leaving Brazil off its list does not make playing lawful: the ban covers operators based abroad that offer bets to people in Brazil.
body: Brazil's Provisional Measure 1.394 of 25 September 2026 prohibits fixed-odds betting nationwide, sports betting and online casino games alike, and the Ministry of Finance says it applies even when an operator based abroad offers them to people in Brazil. The licensed .bet.br sites went offline on 6 October. Crypto casinos licensed elsewhere were never part of that market, so the question is what they do now.

Every crypto casino publishes a list of the countries it does not accept, usually in its terms or help centre. We read that list for each of the 46 crypto casinos we track. The full table, each row linked to the casino's own page, is below, and the same data is a CSV.
## How we checked

On 8 October 2026 we loaded each casino's own restricted-countries page. Where the page builds its list in the browser, we loaded it in a browser. Where a page sat behind a bot check or did not load, we did not get around it: the row shows our earlier reading and is marked that way. A list we count as complete is one the casino publishes in full; where a casino refers to a list it does not publish, we mark it not complete, because a missing name there proves nothing.
## What the lists say

**8 casinos name Brazil.** Four of those pages were re-read on 8 October (BitStarz, mBit, Yeet and Spartans); the other four (Stake, Bitcasino.io, Housebets and Toshibet) sit behind bot checks, so their rows carry our earlier reading.

**25 publish a full list without Brazil.** We re-read 12 of them on 8 October, among them Roobet, Shuffle, BC.Game, Cloudbet and MetaWin; Brazil was not on any. Two needed a closer look: Roobet's page mentions Brazil only in its language menu (Português do Brasil), and 7Bit names Brazil only under restrictions for specific live games and slots, not in its casino-wide list.
**One says Brazil is welcome.** Gamba's page lists the countries it refuses and then says its services are available to users from all other countries, "including … Brazil".
**12 do not publish a complete list**, so whether they accept Brazil cannot be read from their terms.
## Why a missing name matters

For a player in Brazil, a casino's restricted list is not the law. The measure prohibits offering these games to people in Brazil whoever the operator is, so a casino that leaves Brazil off its list is not thereby lawful to play at from Brazil. Our Brazil country pages lead with the ban for that reason and show no casino offers.
The lists matter because they are the casinos' own statement of where they operate. Two weeks in, most of them have not changed it.
## What happens next

A provisional measure has the force of law from the day it is published, and lapses unless Congress converts it into law within 60 days, extendable once by another 60. We will re-read these lists each month while the measure stands, and when Congress acts.

key: Roo Jackpots is an opt-in side bet at Roobet: you add $0.10, $1 or $5 to every bet you place, on top of the bet itself.
Each $0.10 is one attempt at four jackpots. They start at $200 (Mini), $5,000 (Minor), $75,000 (Major) and $250,000 (Mega), and every contribution is split equally between them.
Roobet's own jackpot window says the jackpots average an RTP of 80%. On average, every $1 you contribute returns about 80 cents.
Jackpot wins land in your balance with no wagering requirement. The promotion page runs it from 12 October to 31 December 2026.
body: Roobet launched Roo Jackpots on 12 October 2026. Its promotion page says that within the first 24 hours more than 400 winners landed over $530,000 in jackpot prizes, and that the top jackpot is worth over $1,000,000. Everything below comes from Roobet's own promotion page and its Roo Jackpots terms.
## How it works

You opt in once, in a game or the casino lobby, and choose how much to add to each bet: $0.10, $1.00 or $5.00. From then on that amount is added to every bet and taken from your balance. Bet $1 with a $0.10 contribution and you are charged $1.10. You stay opted in until you opt out, and you can change the amount at any time.
Each $0.10 counts as one attempt. A $1 contribution is ten attempts with a single bet, and $5 is fifty. A jackpot can trigger at random on any of them, and the winner is picked at random.

Contributions count on every game and bet except Roobet's prediction markets, free spins and free bets, bonus-wallet funds, and mid-round side bets such as a blackjack split or double down, where only the first bet carries the contribution. If your balance can't cover the contribution, the bet goes ahead without it.
## The four jackpots

Every contribution is split equally between four jackpots, and each one starts from a fixed seed: Mini at $200, Minor at $5,000, Major at $75,000 and Mega at $250,000. They grow as contributions come in, and the live totals sit on Roobet's site. Roobet describes the Mini as triggering often and the Mega as huge but rare.
## What it costs

Roobet's own jackpot window says the jackpots "offer a highly volatile experience with huge prizes, averaging to a RTP of 80%". That is the figure to keep in mind. On average, $1 contributed returns about $0.80, so the side bet costs about 20 cents per dollar over the long run, before the game you are playing takes its own edge.

At the smallest setting the cost adds up fast. A $0.10 contribution on a $1 spin raises that spin's cost by 10%. Over 1,000 spins you contribute $100, and at 80% you would expect around $80 back from jackpots, spread very unevenly: most players win little or nothing and a few win big. For comparison, the slots on our list publish returns around 96%.
## Worth it?

As entertainment, maybe, as long as you treat it as what it is: an extra bet with a lower average return than the games themselves. If you would rather your money work harder, leave it off and rely on Roobet's standing rewards, such as rakeback, which pays back part of every bet instead of taking more. You can opt out at any time.
## The fine print

Jackpot wins are added to your balance automatically and carry no wagering requirement. Roobet may run extra checks on winners and keeps a prize if a winner won't cooperate. Errors lead to cancelled payouts, and anyone exploiting the jackpots is disqualified. Roobet can pause or end Roo Jackpots without notice; if it does, contributions already made roll into a future jackpot.

key: Gamdom says it detected a potential disk failure on one of its servers, then found an unauthorised connection on one of its automation servers while investigating.
As a precaution it took all of its systems offline. Gamdom says user funds are safe.
Gamdom is back online. Its post apologises for the downtime and lists compensation for all players, including a 20% deposit bonus for existing users.
If you play at Gamdom: check your balance and recent transactions, and turn on two-factor authentication if it isn't on already.
body: Gamdom, one of the crypto casinos we track, went offline in October 2026. Everything below is from Gamdom's own posts on its X account, read on 16 October 2026; we have not seen any other account of the incident from Gamdom or from its regulator.
## What Gamdom said happened

In a post on 13 October 2026, Gamdom said that about 24 hours earlier it had detected a potential disk failure on one of its servers. While investigating, it identified an unauthorised connection on one of its automation servers, which prompted a wider investigation.

"As a precautionary measure, we made the difficult decision to take all of our systems offline in order to fully assess the situation and protect our users," the post said. Gamdom stated that user funds are safe and that it was working to restore services "as quickly and securely as possible". It did not say what the unauthorised connection was able to reach, and we have no information beyond its posts.
## Back online

Gamdom's pinned post now says the site is back online. It apologises for the downtime, thanks its users, and lists compensation for all players: a $45k daily leaderboard, a reload restart, a 20% deposit bonus for existing users and a $45k daily King of the Hill for the week, plus a $50k giveaway on X itself. These are short-term offers tied to the outage; check Gamdom's own promotions page for what is still running and the terms of each.
## What to check on your account
Gamdom says funds are safe. Even so, after any security incident at a site that holds your money, a few minutes of checking is worth it:
**Check your balance and history.** Compare your balance and recent deposits, bets and withdrawals with what you expect. Contact Gamdom's support if anything looks wrong.
**Turn on two-factor authentication** in your account settings if it isn't on, and use a password you don't use anywhere else.

**Keep only what you're playing with on the site.** A casino balance is held by the casino, not in your own wallet. Withdrawing what you are not using keeps it under your control; see our guide to bankroll separation.
## Where Gamdom stands on our index

Gamdom's profile on this site lists its licence, withdrawal times and rewards, each from its own pages. The incident is recorded there too, with the date and source, and we will update both if Gamdom publishes more.
